linkages: CEOs identified within firms from the DISCO occupational code (90 per cent of firm-year observations); otherwise from the occupational code of the highest paid wage earner if in the 'Managers' category; otherwise (11 firm-year observations, 0.17 per cent) the highest paid wage earner

Board members linked to firms through Danish Business Authority filings for the entire population of firms irrespective of firm size, and to each other through co-service on boards (interlocks), monthly
Workers linked to firms through the Integrated Database for Labor Market Research: all full-time employees with their main employment in the focal firm, measured at the end of November each year
Firms matched to industry (NACE-08 first-level section) and to one of four employee-count size brackets to form the CEO pay comparison groups

sample.universe: Danish limited liability firms (Aktieselskaber and Anpartselskaber) that at some point in 2000-2016 have more than 250 employees
selection_rules: Include all limited liability firms that at some point in the observation period are larger than 250 employees (so firms that grow and shrink around the threshold remain in the sample)

Sample period 2000-2016: begins in 2000 because the industry classification nomenclature changed after 1999; ends in 2016 because the CEO-pay-effects analysis needs three years of forward-looking data
Identify the CEO in every firm meeting the size criterion (layered DISCO-based procedure)
Retain only firms where the Chair is uniquely identified in the filings (about 90 per cent of firm-year observations retained)

Locate the entire workforce of each sample firm in the Integrated Database for Labor Market Research; include all full-time employees with their main employment in the focal firm, measured at the end of November each year
For the worker-wage outcome, restrict to the stable workforce, excluding those joining or leaving the company after a CEO pay package is negotiated
sample.n_observations: 6,412 firm-year observations (5,545 in the Table 2 regressions; 5,074 in the Table 3 regressions)

construction_notes: CEO wage premium = natural logarithm of the CEO wage relative to the natural logarithm of the average CEO wage of peers, where peers are defined by industry (columns 1 and 3) or by industry and firm size (columns 2 and 4).
Industry = one of the 21 first-level sections of the European Commission's NACE-08 classification.
Four firm-size brackets based on total number of employees: 250-500, 501-750, 751-1,000, more than 1,000 employees.
CEO wages measured two ways: base compensation = negotiated salary and bonuses; total compensation = salary and bonuses plus long-term incentive payouts including stock and option grants.

Monthly weighted board member-by-board member network: weight 1 if A and B sit on the same board in the same month; weight 0.5 if A and C are connected indirectly through B who serves on another board with C.

Local brokerage_i = local betweenness_i / degree_i, where local betweenness of i is the sum of paths i-j-h with i not directly connected; a threshold of 1 is applied iteratively, sequentially filtering out directors below it.
k-core decomposition run on the subsample of locally nonredundant directors within the largest network component; board members outside the largest component receive k = 0.
Monthly k values standardized by dividing by the maximum k of that period, then aggregated to a yearly value per board member (this is the 'coreness' variable).
Figure 2B plots the director-by-director network of all directors with two or more board positions in 2014.
Worker wage outcome = 3-year growth rate in the firm's average worker wage from t to t+3, measured for the stable workforce; a 3-year window is used to capture wage stickiness.
CEO experience measured as the total number of years the individual has worked as a CEO, from 1996 onwards.
Labour productivity measured as industry-adjusted value added per employee; total assets and number of employees enter in natural logarithms.
Table 1 descriptive statistics refer to 2016 only.

claims.statement: Higher CEO network coreness raises the CEO pay premium (Total pay / Industry adj.).

register_source.value: Danish Business Authority: population-scale board (director) network data

definition.value: Network coreness of the firm's CEO: the k-core value (coreness) in a monthly weighted board member-by-board member network built from all directors in the Danish economy (tie weight 1 if two directors sit on the same board in the same month, 0.5 for an indirect connection through a third director), restricted to locally nonredundant directors (local brokerage = local betweenness/degree >= 1, applied iteratively); the monthly k value is standardized by dividing by that month's maximum k and then aggregated to a yearly value; directors outside the largest network component receive k = 0. A high coreness value indicates high elite status and authority.

timing.value: firm-year t, contemporaneous with the CEO pay premium (both indexed it in Equation (1))

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark registry data (the specific register and variable name are not given in the paper); industry classification from the European Commission's NACE-08

definition.value: The CEO wage premium: the natural logarithm of the CEO's total compensation — salary and bonuses plus long-term incentive payouts including stock and option grants — relative to the natural logarithm of the average CEO wage among peers in the same industry, where industry is one of the 21 first-level sections of the European Commission's NACE-08 classification.

units.value: log points of the industry-adjusted CEO total-compensation premium per one-unit increase in standardized network coreness (0 = periphery, 1 = innermost core)

magnitude.interpretation: These are substantial increases in pay.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on firm and year fixed effects and on the included CEO, workforce and firm controls, network coreness is unrelated to the unobserved determinants of the CEO pay premium (selection on observables within firm).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the controls are included 'to minimize confounding effects' and that the models 'account for endogenous processes such as productivity and individual attributes'; no balance test, placebo or pre-trend evidence is offered.

rhs: unobserved determinants of the CEO pay premium
